faqs.question: Is 보고 싶다 rude?
faqs.answer: Not inherently, but it is not polite either. The Standard Korean Language Dictionary defines its style, 해라체, as a sentence-final form that lowers the addressee to the greatest degree. Sent as a greeting to someone older or senior it is a real social error; used as a caption, a lyric line or a diary entry it is completely normal, because those are announcements rather than address.

faqs.question: Can I just add 요 to 보고 싶다 to make it polite?
faqs.answer: No — 보고 싶다요 is not a form. The 요 particle attaches to the 해체 stem, so the polite version of 보고 싶어 is 보고 싶어요. 보고 싶다 has to be rebuilt rather than extended, and the formal-series equivalent is 보고 싶습니다.

faqs.question: Why do K-pop songs use 보고 싶다 rather than 보고 싶어?
faqs.answer: Because a lyric is an announcement, not a turn in a conversation. The plain style is the form a Korean speaker switches into to mark something as newly noteworthy, which is exactly what a hook line does. It is not the singer quoting a dictionary.

faqs.question: What does 보고 싶었어 add?
faqs.answer: It is the past form in the same 해체 style: 보고 싶었어, "I missed you" or "I have been missing you." The speech level is unchanged — only the tense moves — so the send-to rule for 보고 싶어 applies to it too.

faqs.question: Is 보고파 the same thing?
faqs.answer: 보고파 is a contracted, softer variant of the same construction that learners meet mostly in songs and in playful texting. It sits in the same non-honorific territory as 보고 싶어, so it carries no extra deference and does not fix a register problem.

faqs.question: How many speech levels does Korean actually have?
faqs.answer: Six are standardly listed — 하십시오체, 하오체, 하게체, 해라체, 해요체 and 해체. A peer-reviewed 2026 study in the Journal of Psycholinguistic Research notes that only four are in common modern use, with 하오체 and 하게체 surviving mainly in historical dramas.

faqs.question: Should I write bogosipda or bogoshipda?
faqs.answer: bogosipda. The Revised Romanization of Korean, the national standard published by the National Institute of Korean Language, has no "sh" digraph in its tables. bogoshipda is a spelling-by-ear that spread through fan subtitles, and it is what most of the search results use.

faqs.question: Does the difference matter in a written message at all, or only in speech?
faqs.answer: It matters more in writing, because writing strips the intonation that would otherwise carry the announcement reading. A texted 보고 싶다 to someone you speak banmal with reads as a heightened statement; the same string in a vocabulary app reads as a headword. Context does the work that a rising tone would do out loud.

faqs.question: If both are non-honorific, why does everyone online say one is formal?
faqs.answer: Because 해라체 belongs to the 격식체, the formal series, while 해체 belongs to the non-formal series. That classification is about register, not deference, and repeating it as "more formal" leads a learner to send the least deferential form to the person they most wanted to be careful with.

faqs.question: Is there a Korean form that is safe when I genuinely do not know the relationship?
faqs.answer: 보고 싶어요. It is the only one of the four that the dictionary describes as raising the addressee while staying non-formal, so it works for someone older you are warm with without sounding like a speech. 보고 싶습니다 is correct but reads as public or ceremonial.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Bogosipda vs Bogosipeo: The Difference Is Not Formality

**Bogosipda vs bogosipeo: the difference is not formality.** Korea's Standard Korean Language Dictionary defines 해체 (*haeche*) — the style 보고 싶어 belongs to — as a sentence-final form that does not raise the addressee, and 해라체 (*haerache*) — the style 보고 싶다 belongs to — as one that lowers the addressee to the greatest degree. Both are non-honorific, so neither is polite and neither is safe to send upward. What separates them is discourse function: 보고 싶어 is the ordinary line between two people who already speak *banmal*, and 보고 싶다 is what a speaker switches into to mark a feeling as newly noteworthy. The split lands hardest in writing — only 13.6% of the 214 people who built a miss-you page on SubhSandesh recorded a voice note (29 of 214), and the median written letter there runs 88 words.

On the spelling: *bogosipda* follows the Revised Romanization of Korean, the national standard; *bogoshipda* does not, because the standard's tables contain no "sh" digraph. Our page on [what bogoshipda means in English](https://subhsandesh.in/blog/bogoshipda-meaning-in-english) settles that and the *-고 싶다* construction. This page is only about the ending.

## What the national dictionary actually calls each ending

The Standard Korean Language Dictionary, published by the National Institute of Korean Language, carries a headword for each style, and the definitions are short enough to read whole.

해라체 is "상대 높임법의 하나. 상대편을 아주 낮추는 종결형" — an addressee-honorification style whose sentence-final form lowers the addressee to the greatest degree. Its illustration: 철수야, 빨리 자라. 내일 새벽에 운동해야 한다.

해체 is "상대편을 높이지 않는 뜻을 나타내는 종결형으로, 격식체인 '해라체'와 '하게체'를 쓸 자리에 두루 쓰는 비격식체" — a form meaning the addressee is not raised, used broadly where the formal-series 해라체 and 하게체 would go. 해요체 "raises the addressee to an ordinary degree."

So, in the dictionary's own terms: 해라체 lowers, 해체 declines to raise, 해요체 raises. 보고 싶다 sits at the bottom of that list, not the top.

## Why "bogosipda is the formal one" is backwards

The popular answer has a grain of truth buried in a misleading word. 해라체 belongs to the 격식체, the *formal series*, while 해체 and 해요체 belong to the 비격식체. That is where "formal" comes from.

But 격식 is register, not deference. A peer-reviewed 2026 study of Korean speech style in the *Journal of Psycholinguistic Research* states the classification plainly: "honorific styles include formal and polite styles, while non-honorific styles include half-talk and plain styles." 보고 싶다 (plain) and 보고 싶어 (half-talk) are both in the non-honorific set.

The practical consequence inverts what the learner blogs imply. Send 보고 싶다 to a senior colleague because it looked like the formal one, and you have used the style the dictionary defines as lowering them the most. 보고 싶어요 is the form that actually adds deference.

## 보고 싶다 looks like a dictionary form because 싶다 is an adjective

Here is the mechanism no ranking page explains. Korean 해라체 present declaratives are formed differently for verbs and adjectives: verbs take -ㄴ다/-는다 (보다 → 본다, 하다 → 한다, which is why the dictionary's own 해라체 example ends in 한다), while adjectives take a bare -다.

싶다 is classed as a 보조형용사, an auxiliary adjective. So its 해라체 declarative is 싶다 — byte-identical to its citation form. 보고 싶다 is therefore two things at once: the shape you look up, and a complete finite sentence in the plain style.

That homography is the whole confusion. Learners meet 보고 싶다 in a vocabulary list, meet it again in a lyric, and conclude the singer is quoting a dictionary. They are not — they are using a live ending.

## The switch into 보고 싶다 is a heightening, not a flattening

The common advice is that sending the plain form to someone close reads flat, or quoted. The literature says something more specific, and close to the reverse.

The same 2026 study footnotes the functional rule, attributing it to Lee (1991): "By speaking in non-honorific styles, a speaker switches from the half-talk style to the plain style to communicate the new information which is particularly noteworthy to the listener or to the negative predisposition to the information." The study adds that in practice the two work as one mixed style, "differentiated in terms of discourse function."

Read that against the pair. 보고 싶어 is the maintenance line; switching to 보고 싶다 inside the same non-honorific conversation flags the content as newly striking. The English equivalent is not "I miss you" said stiffly but something nearer "*God*, I miss you." That is why the plain form turns up in lyrics, captions and one-line posts — announcement contexts rather than turn-taking ones.

One correction: this is an *addressee-oriented* information move, not soliloquy. Lee's formulation is explicitly about what is noteworthy **to the listener**. The plain form is not talking to yourself — it is telling someone news.

## Forty-six attested sentences, sorted by ending

Tatoeba's Korean–English corpus returns 46 sentences containing 보고 싶. We read all 46 and classified them by what each sentence ends in, rather than by what it means.

Fourteen end in a finite 보고 싶- form: 4 plain -다, 5 해체 -어, 4 해요체 -어요, 1 합쇼체 -습니다. The other 32 carry it mid-sentence or in a past form.

The asymmetry is in the translations. Five of those 14 are rendered "I miss you" — two 해체, two 해요체, one 합쇼체. **Zero of the four plain -다 sentences are.** All four come out as "I want to see", including 나는 정말 네가 보고싶다 ("I really want to see you") — a second-person object, still not glossed as missing.

It is a small set and we claim no rate from it. But it fits the discourse account: the bare, objectless, addressed 보고 싶어 carries "I miss you," while every plain-form sentence here carries an object and an intensifier instead. Our sibling post cuts the same corpus [by object rather than by ending](https://subhsandesh.in/blog/difference-between-bogoshipda-and-geuripda).

## Which form to send, and to whom

| Form | Dictionary style label | Effect on the addressee | Send it to | Ends a sentence in the 46-sentence Tatoeba set |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 보고 싶다 (*bogo sipda*) | 해라체, formal series | Lowers to the greatest degree | Nobody, as a greeting — it announces: captions, lyrics, a diary line, or a switch mid-conversation | 4, none translated "I miss you" |
| 보고 싶어 (*bogo sipeo*) | 해체, non-formal series | Does not raise | A partner, a close same-age friend, a younger sibling | 5, two translated "I miss you" |
| 보고 싶어요 (*bogo sipeoyo*) | 해요체, non-formal series | Raises to an ordinary degree | Someone older or senior you are warm with; the default when unsure | 4, two translated "I miss you" |
| 보고 싶습니다 (*bogo sipseumnida*) | 합쇼체, formal series | Raises, with formality | Speeches, letters, public messages | 1, translated "I miss you" |

If the question was only *which one do I text my girlfriend*, the answer is 보고 싶어; our guide to [saying I miss you in Korean at three speech levels](https://subhsandesh.in/blog/i-miss-you-in-korean) walks the send-to rule for each.

## What is ranking for this question, and three errors in the top results

We measured the us-en SERP on 2026-09-28 by two routes, and name both, because a position nobody ran is worth nothing. The DuckDuckGo HTML endpoint returned ten results on a `us-en` region call; a US-served web-search index returned its own ten. They agree on the shape: four forum and Q&A threads, six learner blogs, two last touched in 2016 and 2019, and not one dictionary, grammar reference or scholarly source in either set.

Three claims there are checkable and wrong. The top italki answer glosses 보고 싶다 as "verb"; the national dictionary classes 싶다 as an auxiliary adjective. The longest answer on that thread calls 보고 싶다 the "basic way (not conjugated)" — but -다 is a 종결어미, so the form *is* conjugated, into 해라체. That answer also counts five speech styles; the dictionary and the 2026 study both give six. And the highest-ranked learner blog builds its page on an informal/standard/formal ladder of 보고 싶어 / 보고 싶어요 / 보고 싶습니다, never placing 보고 싶다 on it at all — which is why it cannot answer this query.

## What our own data shows, and what it cannot

We can measure how people use our own miss-you template, and nothing more. Across 214 pages built on /missyou-gf since 2026-07-28, 13.6% of senders recorded a voice note (29 of 214) and 92.1% left at least one "open when" letter (197 of 214), 3.2 on average. Those pages have drawn 2,417 views, 11.3 per page, 104 on the most-opened one.

That shape bears on the question: the plain form belongs to announcement and the 해체 form to address, and the written, read-later channel dominates our pages while the spoken one is the minority.

Now the limits, and they are severe. The database records which template was opened; it never records who received it, and nothing is segmented by language or country. No figure above is Korean. viewCount counts page views, not unique visitors — one recipient reopening a page twenty times is twenty views. n = 214 over roughly two months supports no seasonal claim. The city, background-music and "together since" fields are pickers with defaults, so their fill rates are not sender choices, and we have not used them.

## Where our pages help, and where they are the wrong tool

Our [miss-you page for a partner](/missyou-gf) is an English-language product: English labels, English prompts, English furniture. There is no Korean mode. Whatever Korean appears on it is what you type in, so if you cannot yet type Hangul on your phone, the page will not solve that.

It is also the wrong tool for what this article is about. A speech-level choice is one line to one person; if that is all you want, send the line. A page earns its place when the missing is long-running rather than momentary — and for that [Streak](/streak) fits better than a one-off page: two people, one tap a day, a diary neither of you meant to write. Someone who wants a single well-judged sentence needs neither. [Browse the other formats](/templates) if that is you.

## Sources

- Standard Korean Language Dictionary (표준국어대사전), National Institute of Korean Language — entries 해라체, 해체, 해요체
- Romanization of Korean (Revised Romanization), National Institute of Korean Language
- Jung et al., "Differential Effect of Formality of Speech Style on Negation Selection in Korean Children and Adults", *Journal of Psycholinguistic Research*, 2026 — full text read via Europe PMC
- Tatoeba, the 보고 싶 Korean–English set, all 46 sentences read 2026-09-28

The dictionary says the opposite — 해라체 lowers the addressee to the greatest degree while 해체 merely declines to raise them — and a peer-reviewed 2026 paper confirms both are non-honorific and separated by discourse function. Three checkable errors in the top two results are named with the reference that settles each. Against that: the SERP is a Q&A and learner-blog SERP with no authority incumbent, which cuts both ways — it is winnable, but the query is low-volume and none of the first-party data can be segmented by language, so the SubhSandesh figures support the speech-versus-writing argument only by analogy, not as evidence about Korean. Domain authority is far below 90daykorean and HiNative; this is months, not weeks, and no outcome is predicted.

Anti-twin check against the three live Korean siblings. /blog/i-miss-you-in-korean already owns the 해체/해요체/합쇼체 send-to ladder; this post is about the one form that page omits, 보고 싶다, and links it rather than restating it. /blog/bogoshipda-meaning-in-english owns the -고 싶다 construction and the romanisation ruling, which this post compresses to two sentences and cross-links. /blog/difference-between-bogoshipda-and-geuripda owns 그립다 and a Tatoeba count cut by OBJECT; this post's Tatoeba count is cut by SENTENCE-FINAL ENDING, a different measurement on the same corpus, and says so.

Orchestrator claim tested and partly overturned: the row prompt asserted that sending the dictionary form to someone close 'reads as flat or quoted, not intimate'. The peer-reviewed source says close to the reverse — the half-talk-to-plain switch marks information as newly noteworthy, so it is a heightening. The prompt's 'exclamative/self-directed' hypothesis is therefore CONFIRMED as to exclamative and REJECTED as to self-directed: Lee's formulation is explicitly about what is noteworthy TO THE LISTENER, not soliloquy. The post states the corrected version.

Second orchestrator claim corrected: the row prompt glosses 보고 싶어 as '해요-dropped'. 표준국어대사전 defines 해체 as a style in its own right, and defines 해요체 by reference to the slots of 하오체/하십시오체 — not as 해체 plus 요. The post uses the dictionary's framing, not the subtractive one.
